title: Why a 100-Year-Old Mushroom Disease Is So Hard to Stop
summary:
White button mushrooms show up in salads, snacks and everyday meals. But for more than 100 years, growers have struggled with a disease that damages them. Now scientists at the University of Florida think they know why it has been so hard to stop.

The disease is called bacterial blotch. It causes brown or yellow spots on mushrooms, which makes them harder to sell. It can also mean farms grow fewer mushrooms and that the mushrooms spoil sooner. Sometimes the spots do not even appear until after the mushrooms have been shipped to grocery stores.

For years, scientists mainly blamed one type of bacteria. But the new study found the disease is much more complicated.

The research team collected sick mushrooms from several mushroom farms across the southern United States. They used DNA sequencing, which reads the genetic code of living things, along with chemical tests and regular lab tests to figure out which bacteria were present.

"We found more than 17 different species of pathogenic bacteria associated with the disease," said Sameerika Mudiyanselage, the study's lead author. Pathogenic means able to cause disease. Two well-known bacteria were the most common, but the team also found a surprisingly large amount of another group of bacteria that had never been linked to this disease before.

These bacteria can thrive in the humid, carefully controlled indoor rooms where mushrooms are grown. Because many different bacteria may be involved, treatments aimed at just one kind may not work well. That could explain why growers have seen inconsistent results.

Samuel Martins, a plant scientist and co-author, said his team is working on better ways to detect the disease and more sustainable solutions to help mushroom farms across the country.
why_it_matters: Knowing all the bacteria behind a crop disease helps farmers protect a popular food and could lead to treatments that actually work.

background_read: Mushrooms are fungi, not plants, and farms usually grow them indoors in damp, carefully controlled rooms.
Bacteria are tiny living things too small to see without a microscope; most are harmless, but some can cause disease in people, animals or crops.
When a disease is caused by several kinds of bacteria instead of one, a treatment aimed at a single kind may miss the others.
Scientists use DNA tests to tell different kinds of bacteria apart, much like reading a name tag inside each cell.
